newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam daily says opinion divided on reforms.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam daily says opinion divided on reforms.

text.p: A leading Vietnamese newspaper indicated on Monday that rarely reported differences existed within the establishment over the pace of Hanoi's 10-year-old reform process.

A signed commentary in the Quan Doi Nhan Dan (People's Army) daily said diverging veins of thought had emerged between advocates of faster reform and others concerned that reforms might harm socialism.
"Some people are worried that the reforms will mean socialism being lost...some people wish for a faster and stronger pace," it said.
The newspaper added that other groups were seeking new ways to develop reforms and "deviate from reform targets".
The commentary did not directly advocate a solution but said "we should actively smash every plot or activity of our enemies aimed at sabotaging ideology during the reform process".
Suggestions of differences of opinion in Vietnam over key government policies are extremely rare, especially in the country's state-controlled media.
The ruling Communist Party normally goes to lengths to present a picture of unanimity. Government officials have insisted that Hanoi is committed to further reforms.
Western analysts say Hanoi needs to deepen its reform process to avoid losing out to regional competition and to prevent any breakdown in social cohesion.
In a report issued earlier this year, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) urged Vietnam to deepen and renew its commitment to reforms.
"There's a process of change...which, if stability and equity are to be maintained, require a continuation of the reform process," the UNDP said.
Vietnam launched its market-led reform process at a Communist Party Congress in 1986 replacing a Soviet-style command-led system.
The result was an economic lift-off which began in earnest a couple of years later and has brought in some $22.6 billion in foreign investment pledges.
